newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Differences remain on Caspian's status, Kazakhstan.
newsitem.headline: Differences remain on Caspian's status, Kazakhstan.

text.p: Kazakhstan refused on Thursday to join a Russian-led company to develop hydrocarbons around the Caspian Sea and said differences remained over the disputed sea's status.
"It is not to Almaty's (Kazakhstan's) advantage to agree to the (Russian-led) memorandum," said Kazakh Deputy Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Gizzatov, cited by Interfax news agency.

Gizzatov's remarks come two days after Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov appeared to change tack, saying Russia was ready to recognise other states' oilfields outside a 45-mile (72 km) coastal zone.
"Russia is ready to recognise the jurisdiction of Caspian states not only in the coastal zones but also in relation to oilfields situated outside those zones," Primakov said on Tuesday.
At the same meeting, Primakov said Russia, Iran and Turkmenistan would form a company for the joint exploration and exploitation of mineral resources around the Caspian.

Primakov had said Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan were also welcome to join the company. But Gizzatov said Kazakhstan was notified about the new company less than two fours before the start of Tuesday's meeting in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat.
"The company will not operate where Azerbaijan and Kazkahstan's own work is underway," said Gizzatov, quoted by Interfax.

Azerbaijan has also rejected the Russian proposal. Azeri Foreign Minister Hasan Hasanov, quoted by Itar-Tass news agency on Wednesday, said the proposal did not coincide with the republic's interests.
The Caspian Sea was divided up between the Soviet Union and Iran first in 1921 and again in 1940.

But since the break up of the Soviet Union and the birth of three new states along the Caspian's shores, the sea has become the subject of an intense diplomatic and legal battle over the body of water's immense reserves of oil and gas.

The focus of the present battle rages over whether the Caspian is a sea or a lake. Academics argue the sea is actually a salt-water lake but the control of billions of dollars worth of black gold ride on the apparently arcane question.
Russia has previously argued that the sea was a lake whose resources should be developed and shared equally by all the littoral states -- Russia, Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

The Caspian ranks eighth in the world in terms of discovered oil reserves. Reserves in Kazakhstan's continental shelf of the Caspian alone are estimated at 10 billion tonnes. The sea has not been fully studied and may hold much more.
No agreement was reached at the meeting on the Caspian Sea's status but the five countries are due to meet again to discuss the issue in Kazakhstan in December.
